In other words, the cardinality of set \(A\) is strictly less than the cardinality of its power set \(P(A)\), i.e., \(|A| < |P(A)|\).

Proof of Cantor's Theorem (Diagonal Argument)

We proceed by contradiction.

Suppose there exists a surjective mapping \(\phi: A o P(A)\). This means that for every element in \(P(A)\) (i.e., every subset of \(A\)), at least one preimage can be found in \(A\).

Now, we construct a special set \(B \subseteq A\):

\[ B = \{a \in A \mid a otin \phi(a)\} \]

Since all elements of \(B\) are taken from \(A\), \(B\) is clearly a subset of \(A\), meaning \(B \in P(A)\).

Because \(\phi\) is surjective, there must exist some element \(a_0 \in A\) such that its image is exactly the set \(B\). That is:

\[ \phi(a_0) = B \]

Next, we discuss whether the element \(a_0\) belongs to set \(B\). There are only two possibilities:

  • Case 1: Assume \(a_0 \in B\)

By the definition of set \(B\), if \(a_0 \in B\), then it must satisfy \(a_0 otin \phi(a_0)\). However, we know \(\phi(a_0) = B\), which implies \(a_0 otin B\). This leads to a contradiction (\(a_0 \in B \Rightarrow a_0 otin B\)).

  • Case 2: Assume \(a_0 otin B\)

Since \(a_0 otin B\) and \(B = \phi(a_0)\), this implies \(a_0 otin \phi(a_0)\). However, according to the construction of set \(B\), all elements \(x\) that satisfy \(x otin \phi(x)\) must be contained in \(B\). Therefore, we must have \(a_0 \in B\). This also leads to a contradiction (\(a_0 otin B \Rightarrow a_0 \in B\)).

In summary, both cases lead to an irreconcilable logical contradiction. Thus, the initial assumption—"there exists a surjection from \(A\) to \(P(A)\)"—is false. The theorem is proved. \(\square\)

docs.title: 4. Relations and Partially Ordered Sets
docs.text:
In addition to mappings, binary relations on sets are the cornerstones for building complex mathematical structures (such as partial orders and equivalence relations).

Definition 1.4 (Binary Relation and Partial Order)

  • Relation: Let \(X\) be a set. A binary relation \(R\) on \(X\) is a subset of the Cartesian product \(X \times X\), i.e., \(R \subseteq X \times X\). If \((a, b) \in R\), we typically write \(aRb\).

  • Partial Order: Let \(\le\) be a binary relation on \(X\). If \(\le\) satisfies the following three properties, it is called a partial order on \(X\):

  • (1) Reflexivity: For any \(a \in X\), \(a \le a\).

  • (2) Antisymmetry: For any \(a, b \in X\), if \(a \le b\) and \(b \le a\), then \(a = b\).

  • (3) Transitivity: For any \(a, b, c \in X\), if \(a \le b\) and \(b \le c\), then \(a \le c\).

A set \((X, \le)\) endowed with a partial order relation is called a Partially Ordered Set (POSET).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Functions and Relations
docs.text: In the study of point-set topology, mappings between sets (functions) and the internal structures of sets (relations) serve as the fundamental language. This chapter strictly defines functions, equivalence relations, and order relations. These tools will be employed in later chapters to construct topological spaces, quotient spaces, and order topologies.

docs.title: 1. Functions and Their Basic Properties
docs.text:
In set theory, a function (mapping) is viewed as a specific subset of a Cartesian product characterized by the property of uniqueness.

Definition 2.1 (Function/Mapping)

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two sets. A function \(f\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is a subset \(S_f\) of the Cartesian product \(A \times B\) such that: for every \(a \in A\), there exists a unique \(b \in B\) such that \((a, b) \in S_f\).

  • Notation: If \((a, b) \in S_f\), it is denoted as \(b = f(a)\). The mapping itself is denoted as \(f: A \to B\).
  • Domain: Denoted as \(D(f) = A\).
  • Image: Denoted as \(I(f) = \{f(a) \mid a \in A\} \subseteq B\).

docs.title: 1.1 Classification of Mappings
docs.text:
Mappings are classified into the following three categories based on how they cover and distinguish elements:

  • Injective (One-to-one): If for any \(a, a' \in A\), \(a \neq a'\) implies \(f(a) \neq f(a')\).

  • Surjective (Onto): If \(f(A) = B\), i.e., for every \(b \in B\), there exists at least one \(a \in A\) such that \(f(a) = b\).

  • Bijective: A mapping that is both injective and surjective.

docs.title: 1.2 Composition and Identity Mappings
docs.text:
For bijections from a set \(A\) to itself, we have the following properties:

  • Identity Mapping: Defined as \(id_A: A \to A\) where \(id_A(a) = a\).

  • Composition: If \(f: A \to B\) and \(g: B \to C\), then the composite mapping \(g \circ f: A \to C\) is defined as:

\[ (g \circ f)(a) = g(f(a)) \]

docs.title: 2. Relations and Equivalence Classes
docs.text:
Binary relations describe the connections between elements within a set, where equivalence relations are the core for constructing quotient spaces.

Definition 2.2 (Binary Relation)

A binary relation \(R\) on a set \(A\) is a subset of the Cartesian product \(A \times A\). If \((x, y) \in R\), we write \(xRy\) or \(x \sim y\).

docs.title: 2.1 Equivalence Relations
docs.text:
A relation \(R\) is called an equivalence relation if it satisfies the following three properties:

  • Reflexivity (Reflexive): For all \(x \in A\), \((x, x) \in R\).

  • Symmetry (Symmetric): If \((x, y) \in R\), then \((y, x) \in R\).

  • Transitivity (Transitive): If \((x, y) \in R\) and \((y, z) \in R\), then \((x, z) \in R\).

docs.title: 2.2 Equivalence Classes and Partitions
docs.text:
• Equivalence Class: The set of all elements that have an equivalence relation \(\sim\) with \(a\), denoted by:
\[ [a] = \{ a' \in A \mid a' \sim a \} \]
  • Partition Property: Any two equivalence classes are either equal or disjoint. The union of all equivalence classes equals the entire space \(A\).
\[ A = \bigcup_{a \in A} [a] \]

docs.title: 3. Order Relations
docs.text:
Order relations introduce directionality to a set and form the basis for defining the order topology.

Definition 2.3 (Total Order / Linear Order)

A total order relation \(L\) on a set \(A\) is a subset \(L \subseteq A \times A\) that satisfies the following conditions:

  • (1) Reflexivity: \((x, x) \in L\).
  • (2) Transitivity: If \((x, y) \in L\) and \((y, z) \in L\), then \((x, z) \in L\).
  • (3) Comparability (Trichotomy): For any \(x, y \in A\), either \((x, y) \in L\) or \((y, x) \in L\) must hold.

docs.title: 3.1 Lexicographic Order
docs.text:
Let \((A, <_A)\) and \((B, <_B)\) be totally ordered sets. One can define the lexicographic order \(<\) on \(A \times B\): \((a, b) < (a', b')\) if and only if:

\[ a <_A a' \quad \text{or} \quad (a = a' \text{ and } b <_B b') \]

docs.title: 4.1 Mathematical Induction
docs.text:
Let \(P(x)\) be a property concerning natural numbers \(x \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge a}\). If the following hold:

  • (1) \(P(a)\) is true;
  • (2) Assuming \(P(y)\) is true for all \(a \le y \le n\) implies that \(P(n+1)\) is true;

Then \(P(x)\) is true for all \(x \ge a\).

docs.title: 4.2 Finite Sets
docs.text:
• Definition: A set \(A\) is called a finite set if \(A = \emptyset\), or if there exists a bijection \(f: A \to \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
  • Cardinality: If such an \(n\) exists, the size (cardinality) of set \(A\) is said to be \(n\).

docs.title: 5. Preimage and Foundations of Continuity (Tool Supplement)
docs.text:
In topology, we are more concerned with the "pullback" properties of subsets.

Definition 2.4 (Preimage)

For a mapping \(f: X \to Y\) and a subset \(V\) of \(Y\), the preimage of \(V\) is defined as:

\[ f^{-1}(V) = \{ x \in X \mid f(x) \in V \} \]

The preimage operation preserves set operations well:

  • Preservation of Union: \(f^{-1}(\bigcup V_\alpha) = \bigcup f^{-1}(V_\alpha)\)
  • Preservation of Intersection: \(f^{-1}(\bigcap V_\alpha) = \bigcap f^{-1}(V_\alpha)\)

This explains why topological continuity is typically defined by "the preimage of an open set is still an open set."

docs.title: Chapter 3: Countable and Uncountable Sets
docs.text: In set theory and topology, distinguishing the sizes of infinite sets (i.e., "cardinality" or "power") is extremely important. Not all "infinities" are equal. This chapter strictly defines countability, explores the operational properties of countable sets, reveals the existence of uncountable sets through Cantor's diagonal argument, and finally introduces cardinality and the Continuum Hypothesis.

docs.title: 1. Basic Definition of Countable Sets
docs.text:
First, we need to strictly define the categories of set "size," specifically for classifying infinite sets.

Definition 3.1 (Finite, Infinite, and Countable)

  • Finite Set: A set \(S\) is called finite if it is the empty set \(\emptyset\), or if there exists a natural number \(n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\) and a bijection \(f: S \to \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\).

  • Infinite Set: A set \(S\) is called infinite if it is not finite.

  • Countably Infinite Set: A set \(S\) is called countably infinite if there exists a bijection \(f: S \to \mathbb{N}\) (where \(\mathbb{N}\) is the set of natural numbers).

  • Countable Set: A set is called countable if it is either finite or countably infinite.

As a fundamental example, the set of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) is countably infinite. We can explicitly construct a bijection \(f: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}\) as follows:

\[ f(n) = \begin{cases} 2n, & \text{if } n > 0 \\ -2n + 1, & \text{if } n \le 0 \end{cases} \]

This mapping maps the integer sequence \(0, 1, -1, 2, -2, \dots\) one-to-one onto the natural number sequence \(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \dots\).

docs.title: 2. Equivalent Characterizations of Countable Sets
docs.text:
To make it easier to determine whether a set is countable in practical applications, we have the following equivalent conditions.

Theorem 3.1 (Equivalent Conditions for Countable Sets)

Let \(B\) be any non-empty set. Then the following three propositions are equivalent (TFAE):

  • (1) \(B\) is a countable set.

  • (2) There exists a surjection \(f: \mathbb{N} \to B\) from the set of natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\) to \(B\).

  • (3) There exists an injection \(g: B \to \mathbb{N}\) from \(B\) to the set of natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}\).

Proof of Theorem 3.1

(1) \(\implies\) (2): If \(B\) is countable, it is either finite or countably infinite. If \(B\) is countably infinite, by definition there exists a bijection \(h: B \to \mathbb{N}\), and its inverse \(h^{-1}: \mathbb{N} \to B\) is clearly a surjection. If \(B\) is finite, let \(B = \{b_1, b_2, \dots, b_k\}\). We can construct a surjection \(f: \mathbb{N} \to B\) as follows:

\[ f(n) = \begin{cases} b_n, & \text{if } n \le k \\ b_k, & \text{if } n > k \end{cases} \]

(2) \(\implies\) (3): Given a surjection \(f: \mathbb{N} \to B\). For every \(b \in B\), its preimage set \(f^{-1}(\{b\}) \subseteq \mathbb{N}\) must be non-empty. According to the Well-Ordering Principle of natural numbers, any non-empty subset of natural numbers must have a least element. Therefore, we can define the mapping \(g: B \to \mathbb{N}\) as:

\[ g(b) = \min \{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid f(n) = b\} \]

If \(b_1 \neq b_2\), then because the function \(f\) is single-valued, the corresponding minimum preimages must be different; thus \(g\) is an injection.

(3) \(\implies\) (1): Given an injection \(g: B \to \mathbb{N}\). This means \(g\) is a bijection from \(B\) to its image set \(S = g(B) \subseteq \mathbb{N}\). Therefore, we only need to prove that any subset \(S \subseteq \mathbb{N}\) of natural numbers must be countable.

Suppose \(S\) is not finite. We wish to construct a bijection \(\varphi: \mathbb{N} \to S\). We use the Well-Ordering Principle for a recursive definition:

Let \(S_0 = S\).

Define \(\varphi(0) = \min S_0\).

For \(i \ge 1\), let \(S_i = S \setminus \{\varphi(0), \varphi(1), \dots, \varphi(i-1)\}\).

Since \(S\) is an infinite set, \(S_i\) is always non-empty. Define \(\varphi(i) = \min S_i\).

Clearly, the \(\varphi\) constructed in this way maps \(\mathbb{N}\) one-to-one onto \(S\); therefore \(S\) is countably infinite. \(\square\)

docs.title: 3. Operational Properties of Countable Sets
docs.text:
Countable sets exhibit strong closure properties under basic set operations (such as taking subsets, finite Cartesian products, and countable unions).

Theorem 3.2 (Closure of Countable Sets)

  • (i) Any subset of a countable set is still countable.

  • (ii) The union of countably many countable sets is still countable.

  • (iii) The Cartesian product of finitely many countable sets is still countable.

Proof of Operational Properties

(i) Proof: Let \(A\) be a countable set and \(S \subseteq A\). Since \(A\) is countable, there exists an injection \(g: A \to \mathbb{N}\). Restricting \(g\) to \(S\) yields \(g|_S: S \to \mathbb{N}\), which is clearly also an injection. By Theorem 3.1, \(S\) is countable.

(ii) Proof: Let \(I\) be a countable index set, and for each \(i \in I\), \(A_i\) is a countable set. We need to prove that \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is countable. Since \(I\) is countable, there exists a surjection \(g: \mathbb{N} \to I\). For each \(i \in I\), since \(A_i\) is countable, there exists a surjection \(f_i: \mathbb{N} \to A_i\). Define a new mapping \(\Phi: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) as follows:

\[ \Phi(m, n) = f_{g(m)}(n) \]

Clearly, since \(g\) traverses all indices and \(f_{g(m)}\) traverses all elements in the sets, \(\Phi\) must be a surjection. As long as we can prove that \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\) is countable (there exists a surjection from \(\mathbb{N}\) to \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\)), the composite mapping proves the countability of the union.

Lemma: \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\) is countable. Construct a mapping \(H: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) defined as:

\[ H(m, n) = 2^m \cdot 3^n \]

By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (uniqueness of prime factorization), if \((m, n) \neq (m', n')\), then \(2^m \cdot 3^n \neq 2^{m'} \cdot 3^{n'}\). Therefore \(H\) is an injection. By Theorem 3.1, \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\) is countable. This completes the proof of (ii).

(iii) Proof: By induction, we only need to prove that the Cartesian product \(A \times B\) of two countable sets \(A\) and \(B\) is countable. Given surjections \(f_A: \mathbb{N} \to A\) and \(f_B: \mathbb{N} \to B\). Construct a mapping \(F: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to A \times B\) as \(F(m, n) = (f_A(m), f_B(n))\). This is clearly a surjection. Since \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\) is countable, \(A \times B\) is also countable. \(\square\)

Typical Application: The set of positive rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}^+\) is countable. This is because we can construct a surjection \(f: \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1} \times \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1} \to \mathbb{Q}^+\) defined as \((a, b) \mapsto \frac{a}{b}\). Since \(\mathbb{Q}^+\) is countable, it follows that the entire set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) is also countable.

docs.title: 4. Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Diagonal Argument
docs.text:
Not all infinite sets are countable. The Cartesian product of infinitely many countable sets often leads to an "uncountable" explosion.

Consider the set \(S = \{0, 1\}\). Define \(S^{\mathbb{N}}\) as the set of all functions from \(\mathbb{N}\) to \(\{0, 1\}\), which is equivalent to the set of all infinite sequences composed of 0s and 1s.

Theorem 3.3 (Cantor's Diagonal Argument)

The space of infinite sequences \(S^{\mathbb{N}} = \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\) is an uncountable set.

Proof of Cantor's Diagonal Argument

We proceed by contradiction. Suppose \(S^{\mathbb{N}}\) is countable. Then there exists a bijection \(\varphi: \mathbb{N} \to S^{\mathbb{N}}\). This means we can arrange all infinite sequences of 0s and 1s into a list:

\[ \begin{aligned} \varphi(1) &= (x_{11}, x_{12}, x_{13}, \dots) \\ \varphi(2) &= (x_{21}, x_{22}, x_{23}, \dots) \\ \varphi(3) &= (x_{31}, x_{32}, x_{33}, \dots) \\ &\dots \end{aligned} \]

where all \(x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\).

Now, we construct a new sequence \(y = (y_1, y_2, y_3, \dots) \in S^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that \(y\) does not appear in any of the above positions. The construction rule is as follows (i.e., negating the diagonal elements):

\[ y_i = 1 - x_{ii} = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } x_{ii} = 1 \\ 1, & \text{if } x_{ii} = 0 \end{cases} \]

Since \(y\) is an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s, it must be that \(y \in S^{\mathbb{N}}\). However, for any integer \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), the element of sequence \(y\) at the \(n\)-th position is different from the element of sequence \(\varphi(n)\) at the same position (because \(y_n = 1 - x_{nn} \neq x_{nn}\)).

This means \(y \neq \varphi(n)\) holds for all \(n\). This breaks the assumption that \(\varphi\) is a surjection. Contradiction! Therefore, \(S^{\mathbb{N}}\) must be uncountable. \(\square\)

Note: Through binary expansion, one can establish a mapping from \(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\) to the real interval \([0, 1]\), thus strictly proving that the set of real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) is an uncountable set.

docs.title: 5. Cantor's Theorem and Cardinality Theory
docs.text:
Abstracting further, we can compare the sizes of any set and its power set (the set of all its subsets). For a set \(A\), its power set is denoted as \(\mathcal{P}(A)\). For the set of natural numbers, it is not difficult to find that there is a one-to-one correspondence between \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})\) and \(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\) (via characteristic functions).

Theorem 3.4 (Cantor's Theorem)

For any set \(A\), there exists no surjection from \(A\) to its power set \(\mathcal{P}(A)\), and consequently, there exists no injection from \(\mathcal{P}(A)\) to \(A\).

Proof of Cantor's Theorem

We proceed by contradiction. Suppose there exists a surjection \(g: A o \mathcal{P}(A)\). For any element \(a \in A\), \(g(a)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{P}(A)\), i.e., a subset of \(A\). We construct a "pathological" set \(B\):

\[ B = \{a \in A \mid a otin g(a)\} \]

Clearly \(B \subseteq A\), so \(B \in \mathcal{P}(A)\). Since \(g\) is a surjection, there must exist some element \(b \in A\) such that \(g(b) = B\).

Now we ask a question: does the element \(b\) belong to the set \(B\)?

  • If \(b \in B\): According to the definition of \(B\), we must have \(b otin g(b)\). But \(g(b) = B\), meaning \(b otin B\). Contradiction!

  • If \(b otin B\): That is, \(b \in g(b)\). Again, according to the definition of \(B\), an element satisfying this condition must be in \(B\), meaning \(b \in B\). Contradiction!

Either case leads to a logical breakdown (this is similar to the construction of Russell's paradox). Therefore, no such surjection exists. \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.1 Cardinality and the Continuum Hypothesis
docs.text:
Based on injections and bijections, we define the cardinality relationship of sets:

  • Equal: If there exists a bijection \(A \to B\), we write \(\text{Card}(A) = \text{Card}(B)\) or \(|A| = |B|\).
  • Strictly Less Than: If there exists an injection \(A \to B\) and no bijection \(A \to B\) exists, we write \(\text{Card}(A) < \text{Card}(B)\).

We use \(\aleph_0\) (aleph-null) to denote the cardinality of a countably infinite set (i.e., \(\text{Card}(\mathbb{N})\)). By Cantor's Theorem, we can construct an endless sequence of increasingly large cardinalities:

\[ \aleph_0 = \text{Card}(\mathbb{N}) < \text{Card}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) < \text{Card}(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}))) < \dots \]

The cardinality of the set of real numbers is called the continuum cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\), and it is known that \(\mathfrak{c} = \text{Card}(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})) = 2^{\aleph_0}\). Thus \(\aleph_0 < 2^{\aleph_0}\).

Continuum Hypothesis (CH): Cantor proposed a famous question: Does there exist a set \(X\) whose cardinality is strictly between those of the natural numbers and the real numbers? That is, does there exist \(X\) such that:

\[ \aleph_0 < \text{Card}(X) < 2^{\aleph_0} \]

The Continuum Hypothesis conjectures that "no such set exists." Modern set theory has proven that the Continuum Hypothesis can neither be proven nor disproven within the standard ZFC axiom system (i.e., it is independent of the ZFC system).

docs.title: Chapter 4: Open Sets and Topological Structure
docs.text: In previous chapters, we explored the basic properties of sets, mappings, and metric spaces. Based on this, this chapter will start from open sets in metric spaces, gradually stripping away the concept of distance to establish an axiomatic system for general topological spaces, with a focus on the topological characterization of continuity and the construction of bases for a topology.

docs.title: 1. Open and Closed Sets in Metric Spaces
docs.text:
In metric spaces (or distance spaces), the foundation of all topological properties is the concept of a "ball."

Definition 4.1 (\(\epsilon\)-Ball)

Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. For any \(x \in S\) and any real number \(\epsilon > 0\), the \(\epsilon\)-ball centered at \(x\) with radius \(\epsilon\) is defined as:

\[ B(x, \epsilon) = \{y \in S \mid d(y, x) < \epsilon\} \]

Based on the \(\epsilon\)-ball, we can strictly define open sets and closed sets:

Definition 4.2 (Open and Closed Sets)

  • Open Set: A subset \(P \subseteq S\) is called an open set if for every point \(x \in P\), there exists a constant \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(B(x, \epsilon) \subseteq P\).

  • Closed Set: A subset \(C \subseteq S\) is called a closed set if its complement \(S \setminus C\) is an open set.

Basic Examples and Properties:

  • The entire space \(S\) and the empty set \(\emptyset\) are both open and closed.

  • Arbitrary Unions: If every \(A_i\) in the family \(\{A_i\}_{i \in I}\) is an open set, then their union \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is also an open set.

  • Finite Intersections: The intersection of finitely many open sets must be an open set.

Proof: Finite Intersections of Open Sets are Open

We only need to prove that the intersection of two open sets is open, and then the conclusion can be extended to any finite number of sets by mathematical induction. Let \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k\) be a finite number of open sets.

Consider their intersection \(\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\). If this intersection is the empty set \(\emptyset\), the conclusion holds naturally since the empty set is open.

If the intersection is non-empty, take any point \(x \in \bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\).

This means that for every \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}\), \(x \in A_i\).

Since each \(A_i\) is an open set, by the definition of open sets, there must exist a corresponding \(\epsilon_i > 0\) such that \(B(x, \epsilon_i) \subseteq A_i\).

We simply take the minimum of these radii:

\[ \epsilon = \min\{\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2, \dots, \epsilon_k\} \]

Since the collection is finite, \(\epsilon\) must be a real number strictly greater than 0. At this point, for all \(i\), we have \(B(x, \epsilon) \subseteq B(x, \epsilon_i) \subseteq A_i\).

Therefore, \(B(x, \epsilon) \subseteq \bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i\). This proves that any point in the intersection contains an \(\epsilon\)-ball that lies entirely within the intersection; thus, a finite intersection is an open set. \(\square\)

docs.title: 2. Topological Characterization of Continuity
docs.text:
In calculus, continuity is usually described in \(\epsilon-\delta\) language. In more general spaces, we can use open sets to characterize continuity in an entirely equivalent way.

Definition 4.3 (Continuity of Mappings)

Let \(f: S \to M\) be a mapping between two spaces.

  • Local Continuity at a Point: A mapping \(f\) is said to be continuous at a point \(x_0 \in S\) if for any open set \(V\) in the codomain \(M\) containing the image point \(f(x_0)\) (i.e., \(f(x_0) \in V\)), there exists an open set \(U\) in the domain \(S\) such that \(x_0 \in U \subseteq f^{-1}(V)\).

  • Global Continuity: A mapping \(f\) is said to be continuous on the entire space \(S\) if and only if it is continuous at every point in \(S\). Equivalently, \(f\) is continuous if and only if for any open set \(V\) in \(M\), its preimage \(f^{-1}(V)\) must be an open set in \(S\).

docs.title: 3. Axiomatic Definition of General Topological Spaces
docs.text:
Once we base the definition of continuity entirely on open sets, the distance \(d\) is no longer necessary. We can directly axiomatize the concept of "open sets" to define general topological spaces.

Definition 4.4 (Topology and Topological Space)

Let \(X\) be a non-empty set. A topology \(\tau\) on \(X\) is a subcollection of the power set \(\mathcal{P}(X)\) (i.e., \(\tau\) contains some subsets of \(X\)) that satisfies the following three axioms:

  • (1) The entire space \(X\) and the empty set \(\emptyset\) belong to \(\tau\). That is, \(\emptyset, X \in \tau\).

  • (2) Closure under Arbitrary Unions: If \(\{A_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq \tau\), then their union also belongs to \(\tau\). That is, \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \in \tau\).

  • (3) Closure under Finite Intersections: If \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k \in \tau\), then their finite intersection also belongs to \(\tau\). That is, \(\bigcap_{i=1}^k A_i \in \tau\).

The set \(X\) endowed with the topology \(\tau\) is called a topological space \((X, \tau)\). The elements in \(\tau\) are called open sets of \(X\) with respect to this topology.

If the complement \(X \setminus S\) of a subset \(S \subseteq X\) is an open set (i.e., belongs to \(\tau\)), then \(S\) is called a closed set.

Example: Let \(X = \{a, b\}\). We can define a topology \(\tau = \{\emptyset, X, \{a\}\}\). In this topological space, \(\{a\}\) is an open set, and its corresponding complement \(\{b\}\) is a closed set.

Closed sets have properties dual to those of open sets:

  • \(\emptyset\) and \(X\) are both closed sets.

  • The intersection of any number of closed sets \(\bigcap_{i \in I} C_i\) is still a closed set.

  • The union of a finite number of closed sets \(\bigcup_{i=1}^k C_i\) is still a closed set.

docs.title: 4. Bases for a Topology
docs.text:
To describe a topology \(\tau\), we often do not need to list all the open sets within it. Instead, we can generate the entire topology through a smaller collection of sets—a basis.

Definition 4.5 (Basis for a Topology)

Let \((X, \tau)\) be a topological space. A collection of open sets \(\mathcal{B} \subseteq \tau\) is called a basis for the topology \(\tau\) if for any open set \(S \in \tau\) and any point \(x \in S\), there exists a basis element \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) such that:

\[ x \in B \subseteq S \]

From this, it follows that every open set \(S\) in the topology \(\tau\) can be expressed as the union of some basis elements, i.e., \(S = \bigcup_{i \in I} B_i\).

Not every collection of sets can serve as a basis for some topology. The following theorem provides the criteria:

Theorem 4.1 (Criterion for a Basis)

Let \(\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)\) be a collection of subsets of \(X\). Then \(\mathcal{B}\) can be a basis for some topology on \(X\) if and only if it satisfies the following two conditions:

  • (1) Coverage: The union of all basis elements must cover the entire space \(X\). That is:
\[ X = \bigcup_{B \in \mathcal{B}} B \]
  • (2) Internal Consistency: If two basis elements \(B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}\) are chosen, and any point \(x \in B_1 \cap B_2\) is taken from their intersection, then there must exist a third basis element \(B_3 \in \mathcal{B}\) such that:
\[ x \in B_3 \subseteq B_1 \cap B_2 \]

If a collection of sets \(\mathcal{B}\) satisfies the two conditions above, then the topology \(\tau\) generated by it contains exactly all subsets formed by arbitrary unions of elements in \(\mathcal{B}\).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Induced Topology and Basic Topological Operations
docs.text: In topology, we need not only to study given isolated spaces but also to investigate how to naturally construct new topological spaces from known ones. This chapter focuses on the two most fundamental construction methods: subspace topology and product topology. Additionally, we will delve into basic set operations within topological spaces, including the concepts of interior, closure, and boundary, revealing the dual connection between open and closed sets.

docs.title: 1. Subspace Topology (Relative Topology)
docs.text:
When we focus on a subset of a topological space, we can "restrict" the topological structure of the entire space to this subset, thereby endowing it with a natural topology.

Definition 5.1 (Subspace Topology / Relative Topology)

Let \((X, \tau)\) be a topological space, and let \(A \subseteq X\) be a subset of \(X\). We define a new topology \(\tau_A\) on \(A\), whose elements consist of the intersections of \(A\) with the open sets of the entire space:

\[ \tau_A = \{ A \cap S \mid S \in \tau \} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(A) \]

This topology \(\tau_A\) is called the subspace topology induced by \(X\) on \(A\), and the pair \((A, \tau_A)\) is called a topological subspace of \((X, \tau)\). The elements in \(\tau_A\) are referred to as relatively open sets (or open sets in \(A\)).

Subspace topology possesses the property of transitivity. If \(A' \subseteq A \subseteq X\), we can either induce the topology on \(A\) first and then on \(A'\), or induce it directly from \(X\) to \(A'\). These two methods yield identical results:

\[ (\tau_A)_{A'} = \tau_{A'} \]

(Supplementary Note): Not only can open sets be obtained via intersection, but closed sets in a subspace also possess the same structure. A set \(C_A \subseteq A\) is a closed set in the subspace \(A\) if and only if there exists a closed set \(C\) in the entire space \(X\) such that \(C_A = C \cap A\).

docs.title: 2. Product Topology
docs.text: In addition to taking subsets, we can construct new spaces by taking the Cartesian product of two topological spaces.

docs.title: 2.1 Basis for Product Topology
docs.text:
Let \((X, \tau_X)\) and \((Y, \tau_Y)\) be two topological spaces. Consider their Cartesian product \(X \times Y\). We wish to endow \(X \times Y\) with a natural topology.

Definition 5.2 (Natural Basis for Product Topology)

Define a collection of sets \(\mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\) on \(X \times Y\), consisting of all "open rectangles":

\[ \mathcal{B}_{X \times Y} = \{ U \times V \mid U \in \tau_X, V \in \tau_Y \} \]

We can rigorously prove that \(\mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\) indeed forms a basis for a topology on \(X \times Y\):

  • (1) Coverage: Since the entire spaces \(X \in \tau_X\) and \(Y \in \tau_Y\) are open, \(X \times Y \in \mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\). The basis elements clearly cover the entire \(X \times Y\).

  • (2) Internal Consistency: Let \(B_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\), such that \(B_1 = U_1 \times V_1\) and \(B_2 = U_2 \times V_2\). For their intersection:

    \[ B_1 \cap B_2 = (U_1 \times V_1) \cap (U_2 \times V_2) = (U_1 \cap U_2) \times (V_1 \cap V_2) \]

    Since topologies are closed under finite intersections, \(U_1 \cap U_2 \in \tau_X\) and \(V_1 \cap V_2 \in \tau_Y\). This means the intersection \(B_1 \cap B_2\) itself belongs to \(\mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\), naturally satisfying the consistency condition for a basis.

Definition 5.3 (Product Topology)

The topology generated by the basis \(\mathcal{B}_{X \times Y}\) is called the Product Topology on \(X \times Y\), denoted as \(\tau_{X \times Y}\).

docs.title: 2.2 Constructing Product Topology using Bases of Original Spaces
docs.text:
If we do not wish to use all open sets of the original spaces, we can generate the product topology using only their bases.

Lemma 5.1

If \(\mathcal{B}_1\) is a basis for the topological space \(X\) and \(\mathcal{B}_2\) is a basis for the topological space \(Y\), then their product:

\[ \mathcal{B}_1 \times \mathcal{B}_2 = \{ B_1 \times B_2 \mid B_1 \in \mathcal{B}_1, B_2 \in \mathcal{B}_2 \} \]

constitutes a basis for the product topology \(\tau_{X \times Y}\).

Proof Sketch: For any open set \(W\) in the product space and any point \((x, y) \in W\), by the definition of product topology, there must exist an open set \(U\) in \(X\) and an open set \(V\) in \(Y\) such that \((x, y) \in U \times V \subseteq W\). Since \(\mathcal{B}_1\) and \(\mathcal{B}_2\) are bases for \(X\) and \(Y\) respectively, we can find basis elements such that \(x \in B_1 \subseteq U\) and \(y \in B_2 \subseteq V\). Thus \((x, y) \in B_1 \times B_2 \subseteq U \times V \subseteq W\). The lemma is proven.

docs.title: 2.3 Compatibility between Subspace and Product
docs.text:
These two fundamental construction operations are highly compatible.

Theorem 5.1 (Commutativity)

Let \(A \subseteq X\) and \(D \subseteq Y\). On the Cartesian product \(A \times D\), we have two ways to define a topology:

  • Method 1: Take the subspace topologies \(\tau_A\) and \(\tau_D\) respectively, then form the product topology \(\tau_A \times \tau_D\).

  • Method 2: Form the product space \(X \times Y\) with the product topology \(\tau_{X \times Y}\) first, then take \(A \times D\) as its subspace to induce the relative topology \((\tau_{X \times Y})_{A \times D}\).

    These two methods yield exactly the same topology.

(Supplementary Note: Projection Maps): The deep significance of the product topology is that it is the coarsest topology (having the fewest open sets) that makes the natural projection maps \(\pi_X: X \times Y \to X\) (defined by \(\pi_X(x, y) = x\)) and \(\pi_Y: X \times Y \to Y\) continuous.

docs.title: 3. Interior, Closure, and Boundary
docs.text:
In a topological space, we can "approximate" any subset using open and closed sets, thereby defining the interior and closure.

Definition 5.4 (Interior and Closure)

Let \(A \subseteq X\) be an arbitrary subset of a topological space.

  • Interior: The interior of set \(A\) is denoted as \(A^\circ\) and is defined as the union of all open sets contained within \(A\). That is:

    \[ A^\circ = \bigcup_{S \subseteq A, S \in \tau} S \]

    Intuitively, \(A^\circ\) is the largest open set contained entirely within \(A\).

  • Closure: The closure of set \(A\) is denoted as \(\overline{A}\) and is defined as the intersection of all closed sets containing \(A\). That is:

    \[ \overline{A} = \bigcap_{A \subseteq V, V^c \in \tau} V \]

    Intuitively, \(\overline{A}\) is the smallest closed set containing \(A\).

Classic Examples: In the real line \(X = \mathbb{R}\) with the standard topology:

  • Let \(A = [1, 2)\), then its interior is \(A^\circ = (1, 2)\), and its closure is \(\overline{A} = [1, 2]\).

  • Let \(A = \mathbb{Q}\) (the set of rational numbers). Since the rationals contain no non-empty open intervals, its interior is \(A^\circ = \emptyset\). Since rational numbers are dense in the reals, its closure is \(\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: 3.1 Dual Properties of Interior and Closure
docs.text:
Interior and closure exhibit perfect duality via complementation operations.

Theorem 5.2 (Basic Properties and Duality)

For any subsets \(A, B\) in space \(X\), the following properties hold:

  • (1) Duality:

    \[ X \setminus A^\circ = \overline{X \setminus A} \] \[ X \setminus \overline{A} = (X \setminus A)^\circ \]

  • (2) Extreme Equivalence:

    \[ A \text{ is an open set} \iff A = A^\circ \] \[ A \text{ is a closed set} \iff A = \overline{A} \]

  • (3) Idempotency: The interior of the interior is the interior, and the closure of the closure is the closure.

    \[ (A^\circ)^\circ = A^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{\overline{A}} = \overline{A} \]

  • (4) Distributive Laws:

    \[ (A \cap B)^\circ = A^\circ \cap B^\circ \] \[ \overline{A \cup B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \]

docs.title: 3.2 Boundary (Frontier) (Supplement)
docs.text:
With the concepts of interior and closure, we can precisely define the "edge" of a set.

Definition 5.5 (Boundary)

The boundary of set \(A\) is denoted as \(\partial A\) (or \(\text{bd}(A)\)) and is defined as the difference between the closure of the set and its interior:

\[ \partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ \]

Another equivalent definition of the boundary is: \(\partial A = \overline{A} \cap \overline{X \setminus A}\). This means that for any point on the boundary, every open neighborhood contains both points in \(A\) and points outside \(A\). A set is both closed and open (a "clopen" set) if and only if its boundary is empty.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Closure, Continuity, and Homeomorphism
docs.text: After establishing the foundations of topological spaces and open sets in the previous chapter, this chapter will further explore the connections between points and sets in topological spaces (such as closures and limit points), and deeply study the bridge connecting different topological spaces—continuous mappings. We will also introduce the most core equivalent classification standard in topology: Homeomorphism. Finally, we will generalize the concept of product spaces, contrasting the differences between the box topology and the product topology.

docs.title: 1. Closure and Limit Points
docs.text: In Chapter 5, we defined the closure via the smallest closed set containing a set. Here, we provide a more intuitive point-set criterion for closure through "neighborhood intersection."

docs.title: 1.1 Neighborhood Characterization of Closure
docs.text:
Proposition 6.1 (Point-set Characterization of Closure)

Let \(A \subseteq X\) be a subset of a topological space \(X\).

  • (1) A point \(x \in \overline{A}\) if and only if every open set \(U\) containing \(x\) intersects \(A\), i.e., \(U \cap A eq \emptyset\).
  • (2) If \(\mathcal{B}\) is a basis for the topology \( au\), then \(x \in \overline{A}\) if and only if for every basis element \(B \in \mathcal{B}\) containing \(x\), we have \(B \cap A eq \emptyset\).
Proof of Proposition 6.1

Sufficiency (If): Suppose there exists an open set \(U\) containing \(x\) such that \(U \cap A = \emptyset\). This means \(A \subseteq X \setminus U\). Since \(U\) is open, its complement \(X \setminus U\) is a closed set containing \(A\). According to the definition that the closure is the "smallest closed set containing \(A\)," it must follow that \(\overline{A} \subseteq X \setminus U\). Since \(x \in U\), then \(x otin X \setminus U\), which implies \(x otin \overline{A}\). This proves the contrapositive of the original proposition.

Necessity (Only if): Suppose \(x otin \overline{A}\). Let \(U = X \setminus \overline{A}\). Since \(\overline{A}\) is a closed set, \(U\) is an open set containing \(x\). Clearly, \(U \cap \overline{A} = \emptyset\), therefore \(U \cap A = \emptyset\). This also proves the reverse contrapositive. \(\square\)

docs.title: 1.2 Limit Points (Cluster Points)
docs.text:
In calculus, limits reflect the trend of a sequence approaching a point. In general topology, this approach is abstracted as a "limit point."

Definition 6.1 (Limit Point / Cluster Point)

Let \(A \subseteq X\). A point \(x\) is called a limit point of set \(A\) if for every open set \(U\) containing \(x\):

\[ U \cap (A \setminus \{x\}) \neq \emptyset \]

In other words, every open set containing \(x\) must contain at least one point of \(A\) other than \(x\) itself.

We denote the set of all limit points of \(A\) in \(X\) as \(LP(A)\) (commonly also denoted as the derived set \(A'\)).

There is a direct connection between the closure and limit points: \(\overline{A} = A \cup LP(A)\).

Examples: * In the real space \(\mathbb{R}\) (endowed with the standard topology), let \(A = \{\frac{1}{n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\}\). Although \(0 \notin A\), \(0\) is the unique limit point of \(A\), i.e., \(LP(A) = \{0\}\), and \(\overline{A} = A \cup \{0\}\). * Let \(X = \{a, b, c\}\) with the topology \(\tau = \{\emptyset, X, \{a\}\}\). For the subset \(A = \{a\}\), its closure is \(\overline{A} = X\), and the set of limit points is \(LP(A) = \{b, c\}\).

docs.title: 2. Continuity
docs.text:
The continuity of mappings is the most central object of study in topology. Topology discards the dependence on specific numerical differences (\(\epsilon-\delta\)) found in metric spaces and establishes continuity purely on the pullback (preimage) of open sets.

Definition 6.2 (Continuous Mapping)

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a mapping between topological spaces.

  • (1) Local Continuity: The mapping \(f\) is continuous at point \(x_0 \in X\) if for any open set \(V \subseteq Y\) containing the image point \(f(x_0)\), there exists an open set \(U\) in \(X\) containing \(x_0\) such that \(U \subseteq f^{-1}(V)\) (i.e., \(f(U) \subseteq V\)).
  • (2) Global Continuity: The mapping \(f\) is continuous on the entire \(X\) if and only if it is continuous at every point in \(X\).

The following lemma gives equivalent characterizations for determining global continuity, which are used extremely frequently in subsequent proofs.

Lemma 6.1 (Equivalent Characterizations of Continuity)

For a mapping \(f: X \to Y\), the following four statements are equivalent (TFAE):

  • (i) \(f\) is a continuous mapping.
  • (ii) For any open set \(V\) in \(Y\), its preimage \(f^{-1}(V)\) is also an open set in \(X\) ("The preimage of an open set is open").
  • (iii) For any subset \(A \subseteq X\), it always holds that \(f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)}\).
  • (iv) For any closed set \(B\) in \(Y\), its preimage \(f^{-1}(B)\) is also a closed set in \(X\) ("The preimage of a closed set is closed").
Proof of Lemma 6.1

Proof (i) \(\implies\) (ii): Let \(V\) be an open set in \(Y\). Take any \(x \in f^{-1}(V)\), so \(f(x) \in V\). Since \(f\) is continuous, there exists an open set \(U_x\) containing \(x\) such that \(U_x \subseteq f^{-1}(V)\). Therefore, \(f^{-1}(V)\) can be expressed as the union of all such \(U_x\):

\[ f^{-1}(V) = \bigcup_{x \in f^{-1}(V)} U_x \]

Since the union of any collection of open sets is still an open set, \(f^{-1}(V)\) is open.

Proof (ii) \(\implies\) (iv): Let \(B \subseteq Y\) be a closed set. Then \(Y \setminus B\) is an open set. Since the preimage operation of a mapping commutes with the complement operation, i.e., \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus B) = X \setminus f^{-1}(B)\). According to (ii), this is an open set in \(X\). Therefore, \(f^{-1}(B)\) must be a closed set.

Proof (iv) \(\implies\) (iii): Given any \(A \subseteq X\). Since the closure \(\overline{f(A)}\) is a closed set in \(Y\), according to (iv), \(f^{-1}(\overline{f(A)})\) is a closed set in \(X\). Clearly, \(A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A)) \subseteq f^{-1}(\overline{f(A)})\). Because \(f^{-1}(\overline{f(A)})\) is a closed set containing \(A\), by the property that the closure is the smallest closed set, we must have \(\overline{A} \subseteq f^{-1}(\overline{f(A)})\). Applying \(f\) to both sides yields \(f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)}\). (The proofs for (iii) \(\implies\) (i) and (ii) \(\iff\) (i) are similar, completing the logical loop). \(\square\)

Notes: 1. The identity mapping \(id: X \to X\) is always continuous. 2. For an inclusion mapping, if the subset \(A \subseteq X\) is endowed with the subspace topology \(\tau_A\) (the weakest topology making the inclusion mapping continuous), then it must be continuous.

docs.title: 3. Homeomorphism
docs.text:
In the eyes of topology, if two spaces can be transformed into each other through continuous deformation (without tearing or gluing), they are considered identical in topological structure. This "topological equivalence" is precisely defined through Homeomorphism.

Definition 6.3 (Homeomorphism)

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a mapping. If it satisfies the following three conditions, then \(f\) is called a Homeomorphism:

  • (i) \(f\) is a bijection (i.e., injective and surjective, ensuring a one-to-one correspondence between points in the two spaces).
  • (ii) \(f\) is continuous.
  • (iii) The inverse mapping \(f^{-1}\) is also continuous.

If there exists a homeomorphism from \(X\) to \(Y\), we say that the topological spaces \(X\) and \(Y\) are homeomorphic, denoted by \(X \cong Y\).

Examples and Counterexamples:

  • The open interval \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) is homeomorphic to the entire real line \(\mathbb{R}\) (e.g., via the tangent function \(f(x) = \tan(x)\)).
  • Consider the half-open interval \([0, 1)\) and the unit circle \(S^1\). We can construct a bijective mapping \(f: [0, 1) \to S^1\), such as \(f(t) = (\cos(2\pi t), \sin(2\pi t))\). This mapping is clearly continuous and bijective. However, its inverse \(f^{-1}: S^1 \to [0, 1)\) is discontinuous at the point \((1, 0)\) (as points on the circle approach \((1, 0)\), they approach \(0\) and \(1\) respectively in \([0,1)\), causing a tear). Therefore, this mapping is not a homeomorphism! In fact, the compact space \(S^1\) can never be homeomorphic to the non-compact space \([0, 1)\).

docs.title: 4. Infinite Products: Box vs Product Topology
docs.text:
In Chapter 5, we discussed the finite product of two spaces. Now we generalize this to the Cartesian product of an arbitrary infinite family of topological spaces. For infinite products, there are two very different natural ways to construct a topology.

Let \((X_i, \tau_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of topological spaces (where the index set \(I\) can be infinite). We consider their Cartesian product \(\prod_{i \in I} X_i\).

docs.title: 4.1 Box Topology
docs.text:
Definition 6.4 (Box Topology)

Box Topology \(\tau_b\) is the topology generated by the following basis \(\mathcal{B}_b\):

\[ \mathcal{B}_b = \left\{ \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;\middle|\; U_i \in \tau_i \text{ for all } i \in I \right\} \]

That is, the basis elements of the box topology are restricted by the corresponding open set \(U_i\) in every component.

docs.title: 4.2 Product Topology
docs.text:
Definition 6.5 (Product Topology / Tychonoff Topology)

Product Topology \(\tau_p\) is the topology generated by the following basis \(\mathcal{B}_p\):

\[ \mathcal{B}_p = \left\{ \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;\middle|\; U_i \in \tau_i \text{ and for almost all } i, U_i = X_i \right\} \]

Here, "for almost all \(i\)" means that, except for a finite number of exceptions, all other components must be the entire space \(X_i\) itself.

Comparison between the two: Clearly, the basis \(\mathcal{B}_p\) is entirely contained within \(\mathcal{B}_b\). Therefore, the box topology is finer than the product topology (contains more open sets), i.e., \(\tau_b \ge \tau_p\). When the index set \(I\) is a finite set, these two are equivalent (\(\tau_b = \tau_p\)). However, in infinite products, the box topology often causes many topological properties (such as connectedness and compactness) to fail due to having too many open sets, therefore, in modern mathematics, the default topology used for product spaces is the product topology \(\tau_p\).

docs.title: 4.3 Universal Property of Product Topology
docs.text:
Why is the product topology \(\tau_p\) more important than the box topology? Because the product topology is exactly the "minimum cost" to ensure that all natural projection mappings are continuous.

Define the projection mapping for the \(i\)-th coordinate \(p_i: \prod_{j \in I} X_j \to X_i\), whose action is to extract the element at the \(i\)-th position in the sequence.

Proposition 6.2

The product topology \(\tau_p\) is the smallest (coarsest) topology such that all projection mappings \(p_i\) are continuous.

Proof of Proposition 6.2

1. Prove that \(p_i\) is continuous under \(\tau_p\): Let \(U_i \in \tau_i\) be any open set in \(X_i\). Consider its preimage under the projection mapping \(p_i\):

\[ p_i^{-1}(U_i) = U_i \times \prod_{j \neq i} X_j \]

According to the definition of the basis for the product topology, this set is the entire space \(X_j\) in all components except for \(i\) (restricted in only a finite number, i.e., 1 component). Therefore, it is itself a basis element in \(\mathcal{B}_p\), naturally an open set in \(\tau_p\). This proves all \(p_i\) are continuous.

2. Prove that \(\tau_p\) is the coarsest topology making \(p_i\) continuous: Assume \(\mathcal{T}\) is another topology endowed on the Cartesian product, and it is required that all projection mappings \(p_i\) are continuous under \(\mathcal{T}\). Since \(p_i\) is continuous, for any \(U_i \in \tau_i\), its preimage \(p_i^{-1}(U_i)\) must belong to the topology \(\mathcal{T}\). We examine any basis element \(B \in \mathcal{B}_p\) of the product topology \(\tau_p\). By definition, \(B\) is an open set \(U_{i_m}\) in a finite number of components \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k\), and the entire space in the rest. Thus, \(B\) can be written as the intersection of these finite preimages:

\[ B = \bigcap_{m=1}^k p_{i_m}^{-1}(U_{i_m}) \]

Since the topology \(\mathcal{T}\) must contain all these preimage sets, and the topological structure is closed under finite intersections, it must hold that \(B \in \mathcal{T}\). Since every basis element of \(\tau_p\) is contained in \(\mathcal{T}\), the entire product topology generated by the basis must also be contained in \(\mathcal{T}\), i.e., \(\tau_p \subseteq \mathcal{T}\). This proves the minimality of \(\tau_p\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Chapter 7: Mappings in Product Spaces and Connectedness
docs.text: In the previous chapters, we have established the foundations of topological spaces, continuous mappings, and product topologies. This chapter will first supplement the universal property of continuous mappings in product spaces and the concept of metrizable spaces, and then delve into the core topological invariants with strong geometric intuition in point-set topology—Connectedness and Path-connectedness.

docs.title: 1. Continuous Mappings in Product Spaces and Metrizability
docs.text: When studying the product space \(\prod X_i\), we naturally care about how to determine whether a mapping into this product space is continuous. The construction of the product topology (the coarsest topology making all projection mappings continuous) provides us with an extremely elegant criterion.

docs.title: 1.1 Continuity of Mappings into Product Spaces
docs.text:
Let \((X_i, \tau_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of topological spaces, and \(\prod_{i \in I} X_i\) be the product space endowed with the product topology. Let \(p_i: \prod_{j \in I} X_j \to X_i\) be the natural projection mapping of the \(i\)-th coordinate.

Theorem 7.1 (Continuity of Mappings into Product Spaces)

Let \(Y\) be an arbitrary topological space, and \(f: Y \to \prod_{i \in I} X_i\) be a mapping. We define the \(i\)-th coordinate function of \(f\) as \(f_i = p_i \circ f: Y \to X_i\).

Then the mapping \(f\) is continuous if and only if every coordinate function \(f_i\) is continuous.

Proof of Theorem 7.1

Necessity (\(\implies\)):

Given that \(f\) is a continuous mapping.

According to the definition of the product topology, every natural projection mapping \(p_i: \prod X_j \to X_i\) is continuous.

Since the composition of continuous mappings remains a continuous mapping, every coordinate function \(f_i = p_i \circ f\) must be continuous.

Sufficiency (\(\impliedby\)):

Given that for all \(i \in I\), the coordinate functions \(f_i\) are continuous. We need to prove that \(f\) is continuous.

To prove that \(f\) is continuous, it suffices to prove that the preimage of any subbasis element in the product topology is an open set in \(Y\).

The standard form of a subbasis element in the product topology is \(p_i^{-1}(U_i)\), where \(U_i\) is an open set in \(X_i\).

Consider the preimage of this subbasis element under \(f\):

\[ f^{-1}(p_i^{-1}(U_i)) = (p_i \circ f)^{-1}(U_i) = f_i^{-1}(U_i) \]

Since it is assumed that \(f_i\) is continuous and \(U_i\) is an open set, \(f_i^{-1}(U_i)\) must be an open set in \(Y\).

Since the pullbacks of all subbasis elements are open sets, and any open set can be expressed as arbitrary unions of finite intersections of subbasis elements, the mapping \(f\) is continuous on the entire product space. \(\square\)

docs.title: 1.2 Metrizable Spaces
docs.text:
Although topological spaces abandon the dependence on distance, not all topological spaces become "elusive". The open set structure of some topological spaces can actually be entirely generated by some hidden metric.

Definition 7.1 (Metrizable Space)

A topological space \((X, \tau)\) is called metrizable if there exists a metric (distance function) \(d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R}\) on \(X\) such that the metric topology \(\tau_d\) induced by the open balls of the metric \(d\) is exactly equal to the original topology \(\tau\) (i.e., \(\tau = \tau_d\)).

For example, the real space \(\mathbb{R}\) and the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{R}\) are metrizable spaces under the standard topology. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the Euclidean distance \(d_1(x, y) = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_2)^2 + (y_1 - y_2)^2}\) and the maximum metric \(d_2(x, y) = \max\{|x_1 - x_2|, |y_1 - y_2|\}\) induce the same topology, because their open balls can be nested within each other.

docs.title: 2. Basic Concepts of Connectedness
docs.text:
Intuitively, if a space is a "single piece" and has not been split into several parts, we call it connected. We strictly define this concept through the opposite of "separation".

Definition 7.2 (Separation and Connectedness)

Let \((X, \tau)\) be a topological space.

  • Separation: If there exist two non-empty open sets \(U\) and \(V\) satisfying:
\[ U \cap V = \emptyset \quad \text{and} \quad U \cup V = X \]

Then the pair \((U, V)\) is called a separation of the space \(X\).

  • Connected: If there does not exist any separation for the topological space \(X\), then \(X\) is said to be connected.

For a subset \(A \subseteq X\) of \(X\), if \(A\) endowed with the relative topology (subspace topology) is connected as a topological space, then the set \(A\) is called a connected subset in \(X\).

We have the following equivalent criterion for connectedness, which is very useful in actual proofs:

  • Equivalent Characterization: A topological space \(X\) is connected if and only if the subsets in \(X\) that are both open and closed (called Clopen sets) are only the empty set \(\emptyset\) and the entire space \(X\) itself.

Examples Analysis:

  • \(X = [0, 1) \cup (1, 2]\) (endowed with the relative topology induced from \(\mathbb{R}\)) is disconnected. We can take the relative open sets \(U = [0, 1)\) and \(V = (1, 2]\). They are non-empty, disjoint, and their union is \(X\).

  • The set of rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\) is extremely disconnected (totally disconnected space). Because for any irrational number \(\alpha\) (e.g., \(\sqrt{2}\)), we can always use it as a "knife" to cut \(\mathbb{Q}\). Let \(U = (-\infty, \alpha) \cap \mathbb{Q}\) and \(V = (\alpha, +\infty) \cap \mathbb{Q}\). Both sets are relative open sets (and also relative closed sets) in \(\mathbb{Q}\), non-empty, disjoint, and constitute a separation of \(\mathbb{Q}\).

docs.title: 3. Core Properties of Connected Sets
docs.text: Connected sets exhibit excellent preservation properties under common topological operations (such as taking unions, taking closures, and continuous mappings).

docs.title: 3.1 Union of Connected Sets
docs.text:
Theorem 7.2 (The Union of a Collection of Connected Sets with a Common Point is Connected)

Let \(\{A_i\}_{i \in I}\) be a collection of connected subsets in a topological space \(X\).

If this collection of sets has a common point, i.e., \(\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i \neq \emptyset\), then their union \(A = \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is also connected.

Proof of Theorem 7.2

Using proof by contradiction.

Assume that \(A\) is disconnected, meaning there exists a separation of \(A\). This implies there exist non-empty relative open sets \(C\) and \(D\) in \(A\) satisfying \(C \cap D = \emptyset\) and \(C \cup D = A\).

Since all \(A_i\) have a common intersection point, let us take \(p \in \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\).

Since \(p\) belongs to \(A = C \cup D\), then \(p\) must belong to either \(C\) or \(D\). Without loss of generality, assume \(p \in C\).

Now let's examine each individual connected set \(A_i\).

Since \(C\) and \(D\) are open sets in \(A\), \(A_i \cap C\) and \(A_i \cap D\) form relative open sets on \(A_i\), and they are disjoint with their union being \(A_i\). This looks like a separation of \(A_i\).

But it is known that \(A_i\) is connected, and a connected set cannot be separated. Therefore, one of the two sets \(A_i \cap C\) and \(A_i \cap D\) must be empty, and the other must be equal to the entire \(A_i\).

Since the common point \(p \in A_i\), and we have assumed \(p \in C\), there must be \(p \in A_i \cap C\). This implies \(A_i \cap C \neq \emptyset\).

This forces \(A_i \cap D = \emptyset\), which further implies \(A_i \subseteq C\).

This deduction holds for all \(i \in I\). Therefore, the entire union \(A = \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is contained within \(C\).

This means that \(D\) must be an empty set (since \(C \cup D = A \subseteq C\) and \(C \cap D = \emptyset\)). But this contradicts the definition that \(C, D\) must both be "non-empty sets" as a separation!

The assumption is wrong, so the union \(A\) must be connected. \(\square\)

docs.title: 3.2 Closure of Connected Sets
docs.text:
Theorem 7.3 (The Closure of a Connected Set Remains Connected)

Let \(A\) be a connected subset in a topological space \(X\).

If \(B\) is a subset satisfying \(A \subseteq B \subseteq \overline{A}\), then \(B\) must also be connected. In particular, when \(B = \overline{A}\), the closure \(\overline{A}\) of \(A\) is also connected.

This theorem tells us that if you add some (or all) of its limit points to a connected set, it will never become "fractured" because of these newly added points.

docs.title: 3.3 Continuous Mappings Preserve Connectedness
docs.text:
This is the most important theorem for connectedness as a topological invariant.

Theorem 7.4 (Continuous Mappings Preserve Connectedness)

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a continuous mapping. If the domain \(X\) is connected, then its image set \(f(X)\) is also connected in \(Y\).

Proof of Theorem 7.4

Using proof by contradiction.

Assume the image set \(f(X)\) is disconnected. Then there exists a separation of \(f(X)\), i.e., there exist relative open sets \(U\) and \(V\) in \(f(X)\) satisfying \(U \neq \emptyset\), \(V \neq \emptyset\), \(U \cap V = \emptyset\), and \(U \cup V = f(X)\).

Since \(U, V\) are relative open sets of \(f(X)\), their preimages \(f^{-1}(U)\) and \(f^{-1}(V)\) under the continuous mapping \(f\) must be open sets in \(X\).

Observe these two preimages:

  • Since \(U\) and \(V\) are non-empty and both within the image set, the preimages \(f^{-1}(U)\) and \(f^{-1}(V)\) are both non-empty.

  • Since \(U \cap V = \emptyset\), after pulling back, it must also hold that \(f^{-1}(U) \cap f^{-1}(V) = f^{-1}(U \cap V) = \emptyset\).

  • Since \(U \cup V = f(X)\), every point in \(X\) is mapped into \(U \cup V\), therefore \(f^{-1}(U) \cup f^{-1}(V) = X\).

Thus, we have found two non-empty, disjoint open sets \(f^{-1}(U)\) and \(f^{-1}(V)\) in \(X\) whose union is the entire space.

This indicates that \(X\) is disconnected, but this completely contradicts the given condition "\(X\) is connected"!

Therefore, the assumption does not hold, and the image set \(f(X)\) must be connected. \(\square\)

Corollary (The broadest form of the Intermediate Value Theorem): If \(X\) is a connected space and there exists a continuous mapping \(f: X \to \mathbb{R}\), then \(f(X)\) must be a connected subset on the real line (i.e., an interval). This means that for any two points \(a, b \in f(X)\) in the image set, any value \(c\) between \(a\) and \(b\) must belong to the image set \(f(X)\) (i.e., a preimage exists).

docs.title: 3.4 Connectedness of Product Spaces
docs.text:
Theorem 7.5

If both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are connected spaces, then their product space \(X_1 \times X_2\) is also connected. By mathematical induction, the product of any finite number of connected spaces remains connected.

Brief Outline of Proof: Fix a point \(y \in X_2\), the slice \(X_1 \times \{y\}\) is homeomorphic to \(X_1\) and thus is connected. Similarly, for any \(x \in X_1\), the slice \(\{x\} \times X_2\) is also connected. Construct a cross-shaped set \(C_x = (X_1 \times \{y\}) \cup (\{x\} \times X_2)\). Since these two parts intersect at the point \((x, y)\), by Theorem 7.2, the union \(C_x\) is connected. Then we write the entire space as \(X_1 \times X_2 = \bigcup_{x \in X_1} C_x\), and all \(C_x\) have the common part \(X_1 \times \{y\}\). Applying Theorem 7.2 again proves the entire space is connected.

docs.title: 4. Path Connectedness
docs.text:
Connectedness is a topological concept purely dependent on open sets, whereas in intuitive geometry, we usually think "connected" means being able to connect any two points with a curve, which leads to path-connectedness.

Definition 7.3 (Path and Path-connectedness)

  • Path: Let \(X\) be a topological space, and \(x, y \in X\). A path from point \(x\) to point \(y\) is a continuous mapping \(\gamma: [0, 1] \to X\) from the closed interval \([0, 1]\) to \(X\), satisfying the initial condition \(\gamma(0) = x\) and the terminal condition \(\gamma(1) = y\).

  • Path-connected: If for any two points \(x\) and \(y\) in space \(X\), there exists a path \(\gamma\) connecting them, then the space \(X\) is said to be path-connected.

Theorem 7.6

If a space is path-connected, then it must be connected.

Proof Highlights: For any given point \(x_0 \in X\), and for any other point \(y \in X\), there exists a path \(\gamma_y: [0, 1] \to X\). The interval \([0, 1]\) as a sub-interval of real numbers is connected, hence the image set \(C_y = \gamma_y([0,1])\) is a connected subset. And all \(C_y\) contain the common point \(x_0 = \gamma_y(0)\). Therefore, the entire space \(X = \bigcup_{y \in X} C_y\) is the union of a collection of connected sets, so it must be connected.

Note! The converse is not true. A connected space is not necessarily path-connected.

  • Classic Counterexample: Topologist's Sine Curve. Define the set \(A = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) \mid x \in (0, 1]\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). Since \(A\) is the continuous image of the interval \((0,1]\), \(A\) is connected. Take the closure of \(A\) in the plane, \(\overline{A} = A \cup (\{0\} \times [-1, 1])\). By Theorem 7.3, \(\overline{A}\) is connected. However, \(\overline{A}\) is not path-connected. Because the vertical line segment at the origin and the wildly oscillating curve part are "torn" apart, you cannot use a continuous path to cross infinite vertical oscillations in finite time \(t\) to walk from the origin to the curve on the right.

docs.title: 5. Connected Components
docs.text:
When a space is not connected as a whole, we can study the "largest" connected fragments within it.

Definition 7.4 (Connected Components)

In a topological space \(X\), define an equivalence relation \(\sim\):

\[ x \sim y \iff \text{there exists a connected subset } A \subseteq X \text{ such that } x, y \in A \]

This equivalence relation partitions the entire space \(X\) into several disjoint equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the Connected Components of space \(X\).

Connected components have an extremely beautiful closure property: Any connected component must be a closed set. (This is because if a connected component were not a closed set, according to Theorem 7.3, taking its closure would yield a strictly larger connected subset, which contradicts the nature of the equivalence class as a "maximal connected subset").

docs.title: 6. Distinguishing Topological Spaces using Connectedness
docs.text:
Homeomorphisms not only preserve connectedness, but also preserve local connected structures (such as connectedness after removing a point). This provides us with a powerful "topological invariant" tool to prove that spaces are not homeomorphic.

Cut-point Method: If a space \(X\) becomes disconnected after removing a point \(p\) (i.e., \(X \setminus \{p\}\)), we call \(p\) a cut point.

  • Example Analysis: Intervals and Circles are not Homeomorphic

    Consider the open interval \((0, 1)\), the half-open half-closed interval \([0, 1)\), and the unit circle \(S^1\).

    • In the open interval \((0, 1)\), any point is a cut point. After removing any point \(c \in (0, 1)\), the space breaks into two disjoint open sets \((0, c) \cup (c, 1)\).

    • In the half-closed interval \([0, 1)\), after removing the endpoint \(0\), the remaining part \((0, 1)\) is still connected. So \([0, 1)\) has exactly one non-cut point.

    • In the circle \(S^1\), after removing any point, the remaining part (degenerating into an open line segment) is still connected. So \(S^1\) does not have any cut points.

    Since the number of cut points (or the existence of a cut point) must remain invariant under a homeomorphism, and the cut point properties of these three spaces are completely different, these three spaces are pairwise not homeomorphic.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Compactness
docs.text: In point-set topology, compactness is the perfect generalization of the concept of "bounded closed intervals" in calculus to abstract topological spaces. Compact spaces possess extremely excellent properties; they not only guarantee that continuous real-valued functions achieve maximum and minimum values but also impose strict restrictions on the products and mappings of topological spaces. This chapter will explore the definition of compactness in detail, its profound connection with closed sets and Hausdorff spaces, and its preservation under continuous mappings and product spaces.

docs.title: 1. Basic Concepts of Compactness
docs.text:
In calculus, a continuous function on a closed interval \([a, b]\) must be bounded and able to reach its extreme values. To generalize this property to general topological spaces, we introduce the concepts of open covers and finite subcovers.

Definition 8.1 (Open Cover and Compactness)

  • Open Cover: Let \(X\) be a topological space, and \(\mathcal{A} = \{A_i\}_{i \in I}\) be a family of open sets. If the union of these open sets contains the entire space \(X\), namely:
\[ X = \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \]

then \(\mathcal{A}\) is called an open cover of \(X\).

  • Compact Space: If for any open cover \(\mathcal{A}\) of a topological space \(X\), there necessarily exists a finite subcover, i.e., there exist finitely many indices \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k \in I\) such that:
\[ X = \bigcup_{m=1}^k A_{i_m} \]

then \(X\) is called a compact space.

  • Compact Subset: If a subset \(Y\) of \(X\) is compact as a subspace (endowed with the relative topology), then \(Y\) is called a compact subset of \(X\). This is equivalent to saying that for any family of open sets in \(X\) that covers \(Y\), a finite number of open sets can always be selected from them to still cover \(Y\).

Classic Counterexample: The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) (endowed with the standard topology) is not a compact space. Consider the open cover \(\mathcal{A} = \{(-n, n) \mid n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\}\). Obviously, this family of open intervals covers the entire \(\mathbb{R}\). However, if we take any finite number of intervals from it, the largest one will necessarily be of the form \((-N, N)\), which clearly cannot cover the entire real line. Therefore, \(\mathbb{R}\) is not compact.

docs.title: 2. Relationship between Compact Sets and Closed Sets
docs.text:
There is an extremely close connection between compactness and closed sets, especially when the space possesses certain separation properties (Hausdorff property).

Theorem 8.1 (Closed Sets in Compact Spaces)

Let \(X\) be a compact space. If \(Y \subseteq X\) is a closed set, then \(Y\) is also compact.

Proof of Theorem 8.1

Let \(\mathcal{U} = \{U_i\}_{i \in I}\) be a family of open sets in \(X\), and they cover the subset \(Y\), namely \(Y \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i\).

Because \(Y\) is a closed set in \(X\), its complement \(X \setminus Y\) is an open set in \(X\).

We add \(X \setminus Y\) to the original family of covers to construct a new family of open sets \(\mathcal{U}' = \{U_i\}_{i \in I} \cup \{X \setminus Y\}\). Obviously, \(\mathcal{U}'\) covers the entire space \(X\).

Since \(X\) is a compact space, this open cover \(\mathcal{U}'\) must have a finite subcover.

In this finite subcover, removing \(X \setminus Y\) if it exists leaves what must be a finite number of open sets from the original cover \(\mathcal{U}\), and they still cover \(Y\).

Therefore, any open cover of \(Y\) has a finite subcover, so \(Y\) must be compact. \(\square\)

In general topological spaces, compact sets are not necessarily closed (for example, in a trivial topology). However, if we add the Hausdorff separation axiom, compact sets are necessarily closed.

Theorem 8.2 (Compact Sets in Hausdorff Spaces)

Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff space. If \(Y \subseteq X\) is a compact subset, then \(Y\) must be a closed set in \(X\).

Proof of Theorem 8.2

We need to prove that the complement \(X \setminus Y\) of \(Y\) is an open set. Take any point \(x \in X \setminus Y\).

Because \(X\) is a Hausdorff space, for any point \(y \in Y\) in \(Y\), point \(x\) and point \(y\) are two distinct points; therefore, disjoint open neighborhoods exist: there exists an open set \(U_y\) containing \(x\) and an open set \(V_y\) containing \(y\) such that:

\[ U_y \cap V_y = \emptyset \]

When we let \(y\) traverse the entire \(Y\), the family of sets \(\{V_y \mid y \in Y\}\) clearly constitutes an open cover of \(Y\).

Because \(Y\) is a compact set, there exist finitely many points \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_k \in Y\) such that the corresponding finite number of open sets cover \(Y\):

\[ Y \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^k V_{y_i} \]

For these finitely many points, they correspond respectively to the finite number of open sets \(U_{y_1}, U_{y_2}, \dots, U_{y_k}\) containing \(x\). We take their intersection:

\[ U = \bigcap_{i=1}^k U_{y_i} \]

Since this is an intersection of finitely many open sets, \(U\) is still an open set containing \(x\).

More importantly, because \(U_{y_i} \cap V_{y_i} = \emptyset\) for every \(i\), the intersection \(U\) does not intersect any of the \(V_{y_i}\). Thus \(U\) does not intersect the union of the finite cover, and naturally does not intersect \(Y\):

\[ U \cap Y = \emptyset \]

This means \(x \in U \subseteq X \setminus Y\). Because an open neighborhood \(U\) completely contained in the complement can be found for any point \(x\) in the complement, \(X \setminus Y\) is an open set, and thus \(Y\) is a closed set. \(\square\)

docs.title: 3. Compactness and Continuous Mappings
docs.text:
The core of topology lies in studying how continuous mappings preserve the structure of a space. Just as continuous mappings can maintain connectedness, they also perfectly preserve compactness.

Theorem 8.3 (Continuous Mappings Preserve Compactness)

Let \(f: X \to Y\) be a continuous mapping between topological spaces. If the domain \(X\) is compact, then the image set \(f(X)\) is also compact in \(Y\).

Proof of Theorem 8.3

Let \(\mathcal{V} = \{V_i\}_{i \in I}\) be an open cover of the image set \(f(X)\) in \(Y\) (\(V_i\) are open sets in \(Y\)).

Since \(f\) is a continuous mapping, the preimage \(f^{-1}(V_i)\) of the open set \(V_i\) under \(f\) must be an open set in the domain \(X\).

Since \(\{V_i\}_{i \in I}\) covers \(f(X)\), their family of preimages \(\{f^{-1}(V_i)\}_{i \in I}\) constitutes an open cover of the entire space \(X\), namely:

\[ X = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(V_i) \]

\(X\) is known to be a compact space; therefore, this open cover must have a finite subcover. There exist finitely many indices \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k \in I\) such that:

\[ X = \bigcup_{m=1}^k f^{-1}(V_{i_m}) \]

Applying the mapping \(f\) to both sides of the equation simultaneously, we obtain:

\[ f(X) = f\left(\bigcup_{m=1}^k f^{-1}(V_{i_m})\right) \subseteq \bigcup_{m=1}^k V_{i_m} \]

This finds a finite subcover of the image set \(f(X)\). Therefore, \(f(X)\) is compact. \(\square\)

Generalization of the Extreme Value Theorem: If \(X\) is a compact space and there exists a continuous real-valued function \(f: X \to \mathbb{R}\), it is known from Theorem 8.3 that \(f(X)\) is a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}\). In \(\mathbb{R}\), compact sets are equivalent to bounded closed sets (Heine-Borel Theorem). Since \(f(X)\) is bounded and closed, it must contain its supremum and infimum; that is, the function \(f\) must be able to achieve a maximum value and a minimum value on the compact space \(X\).

Combining Theorems 8.1, 8.2, and 8.3, we can derive a corollary that is extremely important in the classification of topological spaces:

Theorem 8.4 (Continuous Bijection from a Compact Space to a Hausdorff Space is a Homeomorphism)

Let \(X\) be a compact space and \(Y\) be a Hausdorff space. If \(f: X \to Y\) is a continuous bijection, then \(f\) must be a homeomorphism.

Proof of Theorem 8.4

\(f\) is known to be bijective and continuous. To prove that \(f\) is a homeomorphism, it only needs to be proven that the inverse mapping \(f^{-1}: Y \to X\) is also continuous.

This is equivalent to proving: for any closed set \(A\) in \(X\), its "preimage" under \(f^{-1}\)—which is \(f(A)\)—must be a closed set in \(Y\). This is referred to as mapping \(f\) being a "closed map."

  • Let \(A \subseteq X\) be any closed set.

  • Because \(X\) is a compact space, according to Theorem 8.1, the closed subset \(A\) is also compact.

  • Because \(f\) is continuous, according to Theorem 8.3, the continuous image \(f(A)\) of the compact set \(A\) is also compact.

  • Because the codomain \(Y\) is a Hausdorff space, according to Theorem 8.2, the compact subset \(f(A)\) must be a closed set in \(Y\).

Since \(f(A)\) is a closed set for any closed set \(A\), the inverse mapping \(f^{-1}\) is continuous. Therefore, \(f\) is a homeomorphism. \(\square\)

docs.title: 4. Compactness of Product Spaces and the Tube Lemma
docs.text:
The finite product of two compact spaces remains compact. This is intuitively obvious (for example, the product of two bounded closed intervals is a bounded closed rectangle), but in a general topological proof, we need to rely on a powerful tool: the "Tube Lemma."

引理 8.1 (Tube Lemma)

Let \(X\) be any topological space and \(Y\) be a compact space. If an open set \(N\) exists in the product space \(X \times Y\) that contains an entire "vertical slice" \(\{x_0\} \times Y\) generated by point \(x_0 \in X\), namely:

\[ \{x_0\} \times Y \subseteq N \]

then there must exist an open neighborhood \(W\) of \(x_0\) in \(X\) such that the corresponding entire "tubular region" \(W \times Y\) is completely contained within \(N\), namely:

\[ W \times Y \subseteq N \]

With the Tube Lemma, we can naturally prove the compactness of the product.

Theorem 8.5 (Compactness of Finite Products)

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) both be compact spaces; then the Cartesian product \(X \times Y\) endowed with the product topology must also be a compact space.

Proof of Theorem 8.5

Let \(\mathcal{A} = \{A_i\}_{i \in I}\) be any open cover of the product space \(X \times Y\).

First, fix any point \(x \in X\) in the domain \(X\). Examine the "slice" \(\{x\} \times Y\).

Since \(\{x\} \times Y\) is homeomorphic to the compact space \(Y\), \(\{x\} \times Y\) is also compact.

Since the slice is compact and \(\mathcal{A}\) covers the entire space and naturally also covers the slice, there must exist finitely many open sets \(A_{i_1}, A_{i_2}, \dots, A_{i_m} \in \mathcal{A}\) covering the slice \(\{x\} \times Y\).

Let the union of these finitely many open sets be \(N_x = \bigcup_{k=1}^m A_{i_k}\). Obviously, \(N_x\) is an open set containing the slice \(\{x\} \times Y\).

At this point, apply the Tube Lemma: there exists an open neighborhood \(W_x\) of \(x\) in \(X\) such that:

\[ W_x \times Y \subseteq N_x \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^m A_{i_k} \]

This indicates that for every \(x \in X\), an open neighborhood \(W_x\) containing \(x\) exists such that the entire "tubular region" \(W_x \times Y\) can be covered by a finite number of open sets from the original open cover \(\mathcal{A}\).

Now let \(x\) traverse the entire \(X\); the family of sets \(\{W_x \mid x \in X\}\) clearly constitutes an open cover of \(X\).

Utilizing the prerequisite condition: \(X\) is also a compact space. Therefore, finitely many points \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p \in X\) exist such that the corresponding finite number of open neighborhoods cover \(X\):

\[ X = \bigcup_{j=1}^p W_{x_j} \]

Then the entire product space can be written as the union of these finitely many "tubular regions":

\[ X \times Y = \bigcup_{j=1}^p (W_{x_j} \times Y) \]

Because each \(W_{x_j} \times Y\) can be covered by a finite number of open sets in \(\mathcal{A}\), the total union of these finitely many "tubular regions" \(X \times Y\) can also be covered by a finite number of open sets in \(\mathcal{A}\).

This proves that any open cover of \(X \times Y\) has a finite subcover; thus \(X \times Y\) is a compact space. \(\square\)

(Note: Through mathematical induction, the product of any finite number of compact spaces is compact. The conclusion that generalizes this to the product of an infinite number of compact spaces remaining compact—the famous Tychonoff Theorem—will rely on more complex set-theoretic tools, such as the Axiom of Choice and the Finite Intersection Property.)

docs.title: Exercise Set 1 (Homework 01 & 02)
docs.text: This section contains the problems and detailed solutions for the first and second homework assignments of the Point-Set Topology course.

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Let \(A\) be a non-empty finite set. Let \(\mathcal{P}(A) = \{A' \mid A' \subseteq A\}\) be the power set of \(A\). Let \(2^A\) denote the set of all functions of the form \(f: A \to \{\pm 1\}\).

Prove: There exists a bijection between \(\mathcal{P}(A)\) and \(2^A\), and calculate the cardinality of \(\mathcal{P}(A)\).

Solution

We can construct a bijection by defining an indicator function (characteristic function).

1. Construct the mapping: Define the mapping \(\Phi: \mathcal{P}(A) \to 2^A\). For any subset \(A' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\), its corresponding function \(f_{A'} = \Phi(A')\) is defined as follows:

\[ f_{A'}(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & x \in A' \\ -1, & x \notin A' \end{cases} \]

2. Prove \(\Phi\) is injective: Assume that for \(A_1', A_2' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\), we have \(\Phi(A_1') = \Phi(A_2')\). This means that for all \(x \in A\), \(f_{A_1'}(x) = f_{A_2'}(x)\). According to the definition of \(f_{A'}\): If \(x \in A_1'\), then \(f_{A_1'}(x) = 1\), and thus \(f_{A_2'}(x) = 1\), which by definition implies \(x \in A_2'\). Therefore, \(A_1' \subseteq A_2'\). Similarly, we can obtain \(A_2' \subseteq A_1'\). Therefore \(A_1' = A_2'\), so the mapping is injective.

3. Prove \(\Phi\) is surjective: For any function \(g \in 2^A\), where \(g: A \to \{\pm 1\}\). We can construct the set \(A_g' = \{x \in A \mid g(x) = 1\}\). Clearly \(A_g' \subseteq A\), i.e., \(A_g' \in \mathcal{P}(A)\). By construction, the function generated by \(\Phi(A_g')\) takes \(1\) when \(x \in A_g'\), and \(-1\) otherwise, which is exactly consistent with the values of \(g\). Therefore \(\Phi(A_g') = g\), so the mapping is surjective.

4. Calculate the cardinality: Since a bijection exists, \(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = |2^A|\). For a finite set \(A\), let \(|A| = n\). When constructing the function \(f: A \to \{-1, 1\}\), for every element \(x\) in \(A\), there are \(2\) value choices (\(1\) or \(-1\)). According to the multiplication principle, the total number of functions is:

\[ |2^A| = \underbrace{2 \times 2 \times \dots \times 2}_{n \text{ times}} = 2^n \]

Therefore, the cardinality of the power set is \(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}\).

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
